security_spec.violation_condition: KVM context-switches hstatus between VCPUs without saving/restoring hstatus.MTAG_I, or the kernel writes a synthesized sstatus/mstatus value (e.g., during signal frame setup, ptrace register set, or user_regs recovery) that corrupts MTAG_I, causing one execution context to inherit another context's code-page tag state
security_spec.vulnerability_pattern: save/restore of sstatus/mstatus/hstatus without MTAG_I mask; __fswrite sstatus CSR without MTAG_I preservation; KVM vcpu switch omitting hstatus.MTAG_I in the save/restore sequence
security_spec.summary: hstatus.MTAG_I and mstatus.MTAG_I are new Zimt CSR bits deposited by hardware on trap entry (HS-mode and M-mode respectively); if the kernel's context-switch or register-save paths omit these bits, a guest VM or process can inherit stale MTAG_I state from a prior context, suppressing tag checks on HLV/HSV emulated accesses and defeating the memory-tagging security boundary

findings.finding: Trap entry uses csrrc (read-modify-write with bit-clear) to clear SR_SUM|SR_FS_VS from sstatus. This preserves all other sstatus fields including any hypothetical MTAG_I. The read-back value s1 (includes MTAG_I) is saved to PT_STATUS(sp) via REG_S at line 190.
findings.snippet:
li t0, SR_SUM | SR_FS_VS
csrrc s1, CSR_STATUS, t0
// ... s1 saved to stack
REG_S s1, PT_STATUS(sp)

findings.finding: ret_from_exception restores sstatus from pt_regs->status with a full csrw. Since pt_regs->status was populated on trap entry from the hardware CSR (which includes MTAG_I), and is preserved through in-memory modifications (signal, kprobes, ptrace all preserve it), MTAG_I survives the save→modify→restore cycle.

Context switch saves full sstatus (with any MTAG_I) to prev->thread, then loads next->thread and isolates only SR_SUM via AND, applying it with csrs (bit-set). Since csrs with register operand does read-modify-write (OR), MTAG_I is preserved in current hardware sstatus. User-mode MTAG_I is later restored by ret_from_exception csrw when the task resumes userspace.
findings.snippet:
csrr  s0, CSR_STATUS
REG_S s0, TASK_THREAD_SUM_RA(a3)  // save full sstatus
// ...
REG_L s0,  TASK_THREAD_SUM_RA(a4)
li    s1,  SR_SUM
and   s0,  s0, s1                  // isolate SUM only
csrs  CSR_STATUS, s0             // bit-set SUM, preserve all other bits

findings.finding: KVM vCPU switch uses csrrw (atomic swap) to cross host/guest sstatus at line 48 and 155. The old host sstatus (with MTAG_I) is captured in t0 and saved to KVM_ARCH_HOST_SSTATUS. On guest exit, host sstatus from memory is swapped back via csrrw, capturing the guest sstatus (with guest MTAG_I) into t2 which is then saved to KVM_ARCH_GUEST_SSTATUS. Both MTAG_I values survive the atomic swap.
findings.snippet:
REG_L t0, (KVM_ARCH_GUEST_SSTATUS)(a0)
csrrw t0, CSR_SSTATUS, t0    // swap: host→t0, guest→hw
REG_S t0, (KVM_ARCH_HOST_SSTATUS)(a0)

findings.finding: VCPU run loop swaps host/guest hstatus using csr_swap(CSR_HSTATUS, ...) at lines 819/839/845/849. csr_swap (csrrw) is an atomic read-then-write: old hstatus (including MTAG_I) is returned and saved to the host context, while guest hstatus is written. On exit the reverse swap restores host hstatus. MTAG_I in hstatus is preserved through the atomic read-modify-write semantics.

HLV/HSV unpriv read path saves old hstatus via csr_swap (atomic capture of current hstatus including MTAG_I), later restores it via csr_write(CSR_HSTATUS, old_hstatus). The old_hstatus value was directly read from hardware, so MTAG_I is preserved.

Signal frame save/restore copies the entire struct pt_regs (including status with MTAG_I) via copy_to_user/copy_from_user. sc_regs is architecturally compatible with the prefix of pt_regs, so MTAG_I in regs->status survives signal delivery and sigreturn.

start_thread() synthesizes regs->status = SR_PIE for execve(2). This deliberately discards the old process's MTAG_I state, which is correct — exec replaces the address space, so stale code-page tags have no meaning. The new process gets a clean sstatus; when the extension is actually supported, this is the correct place to set initial MTAG_I for the new binary.

copy_thread for fork/clone copies parent's full pt_regs including status (line 268: *childregs = *(current_pt_regs())), so the child inherits the parent's MTAG_I. For kernel threads, a synthetic status = SR_PP|SR_PIE is used — correct since kernel threads never have user MTAG_I.
findings.snippet:
*childregs = *(current_pt_regs());              // user fork: inherit parent
childregs->status = SR_PP | SR_PIE;             // kernel thread: fresh

findings.finding: KVM FP save/restore functions use a snapshot pattern: read current sstatus (with MTAG_I) into t2, csrs to enable FS, do FP operations, then csrw CSR_SSTATUS, t2 to restore the exact prior sstatus value. Since t2 was read directly from hardware (which carries MTAG_I), the restore preserves it. This is safe assuming interrupt-disabled context during FP save/restore.
findings.snippet:
csrr t2, CSR_SSTATUS           // snapshot with MTAG_I
li t1, SR_FS
csrs CSR_SSTATUS, t1           // enable FS (bit-set, preserves MTAG_I)
// ... FP operations ...
csrw CSR_SSTATUS, t2           // restore exact snapshot (includes MTAG_I)
